title: Pillar VI — Git Workflows, Testing & CI/CD

sections.heading: Commits and branches: the mental model
paragraphs: A git commit is a snapshot of the whole project plus a pointer to its parent commit — history is a chain of snapshots, not a pile of diffs. A branch is nothing but a movable label pointing at a commit; creating one is instant and free.

The working cycle: edit files (working directory), `git add` selects changes into the staging area, `git commit` seals the staged snapshot. The staging area exists so you can commit a *coherent subset* of your current mess.
Good commits are atomic — one logical change with a message explaining *why*. 'Fix login redirect for expired sessions' can be reviewed, reverted, and bisected; 'wip stuff' cannot.

variants.question: What actually happens when you run `git branch feature-x`?
options: A new label is created pointing at the current commit — nothing is copied
All uncommitted changes move to the new branch automatically
A remote branch is created on origin
The entire project is copied into a new directory for the branch
variants.rationale: Branches are ~40-byte pointers into the commit graph. That's why branching in git is instant and why workflows built on many short-lived branches are practical — there is no duplication to pay for.
optionExplanations: Correct — a branch is a movable pointer, nothing more.
Uncommitted changes belong to the working directory, which is independent of branch pointers (they follow you until committed).
Nothing touches the network until you push — git branch is purely local.
That's how some pre-git systems felt; git branches share the same object store — zero copying.
variants.interviewTip: 'A branch is just a pointer to a commit' is a one-sentence answer that instantly signals you understand git's model rather than memorized commands.

variants.question: You're on `main` with two files edited but not yet committed. You run `git checkout -b hotfix` and then `git commit -am 'patch'`. Where did that new commit land, and what happened to `main`?
options: The commit landed on `main`, and `hotfix` is an empty copy waiting for its first change
The commit landed on `hotfix`; `main` still points at the commit it did before, now one behind
Both `main` and `hotfix` advanced to the new commit, since they started from the same place
The edits were lost during checkout because they weren't committed before switching branches
variants.rationale: `checkout -b hotfix` created a label at the same commit as `main` and moved HEAD onto it, carrying the uncommitted edits along. The commit advances only the branch HEAD points at — `hotfix` — while `main` stays frozen at the older commit. Branches diverge precisely because a commit moves one pointer, not all of them.
optionExplanations: HEAD moved to `hotfix` on creation, so the commit lands there, not on `main` — and it isn't empty, it carried the working-directory edits.
Correct — the commit only advances the branch HEAD is on (`hotfix`); `main` is left one commit behind.
A commit advances a single pointer — the one HEAD references — never two branches at once.
Uncommitted edits follow you across a checkout when there's no conflict; they were never lost.
variants.interviewTip: Say it as 'a commit only moves the branch HEAD is currently on' — that one line explains divergence, fast-forwards, and why other branches don't magically update.

sections.heading: Merge vs rebase — and the golden rule
paragraphs: `merge` ties two histories together with a merge commit — truthful, but busy repos accumulate a criss-cross graph. `rebase` replays your commits on top of the target branch, yielding a straight line — cleaner, but the replayed commits are *new* commits with new hashes.

That rewrite is why the golden rule exists: never rebase commits that others may have based work on (i.e., anything pushed to a shared branch). Rebase your local feature branch freely; rebase shared history and every collaborator's tree diverges from yours.
A very common team workflow: rebase your feature branch onto main to stay current while developing, then merge (often squash-merge) into main via pull request.

variants.question: A teammate rebased the shared `develop` branch and force-pushed it. Everyone's local `develop` now 'has diverged'. What did the rebase do that caused this?
options: Nothing — divergence warnings are cosmetic and safe to ignore
It deleted everyone's commits from the server permanently
It rewrote the branch's commits as new commits with new hashes, so every clone's history no longer matches the remote's
It merged develop into every open feature branch
variants.rationale: Rebase creates replacement commits; force-push made the remote point at the rewritten line. Every local clone still holds the old line, so git correctly reports divergence — and anyone who naively merges the two lines resurrects zombie duplicate commits. This is precisely why shared branches are rebase-forbidden.
optionExplanations: Ignoring it and pulling merges the old and new lines together — the graph doubles its commits and the mess compounds.
The old commits still exist in clones and reflogs — the damage is divergence and duplication risk, not immediate deletion.
Correct — rewritten hashes + force-push = every collaborator's history contradicts the remote.
Rebase touches one branch's history; it never fans out into other branches.
variants.interviewTip: When asked merge vs rebase, don't pick a side — state the policy: 'rebase private history for cleanliness, merge shared history for safety, never force-push shared branches.'

variants.question: Your feature branch is 6 commits ahead of `main`, all still local and unpushed. `main` moved ahead with 3 new commits. You want your feature to sit cleanly on top of the latest `main` with no merge commit. Which is safe and appropriate here — and why?
options: Nothing is safe here; any history operation on a branch behind `main` risks corrupting the shared repo
`git rebase main` but only after force-pushing the feature branch first so the remote is authoritative
`git merge main` into the feature branch, because merging is always the safer default
`git rebase main` on your feature branch, because the commits are private and unshared, so rewriting their hashes harms no one
variants.rationale: The golden rule forbids rebasing *shared* history — commits others may have built on. These 6 commits are local and unpushed, so nobody else has them; rewriting their hashes onto the new `main` tip is exactly the sanctioned use of rebase, giving the straight-line history you asked for with zero merge commit.
optionExplanations: The golden rule only restricts *shared* history; local unpushed commits are the textbook case where rebase is encouraged.
Force-pushing before rebasing is backwards and pointless here — the branch is unshared, so there's nothing on the remote to force over.
Merging is safe but produces the merge commit you explicitly wanted to avoid; 'always safer' ignores that rebasing private history is perfectly safe.
Correct — private, unpushed commits are yours alone to rewrite; rebase gives the clean linear result the golden rule permits.
variants.interviewTip: The trap is 'rebase = dangerous'. Reframe it as 'rebase = dangerous only on shared history' — for local, unpushed work it's the recommended way to stay current.

sections.heading: Unit testing with Vitest
paragraphs: A unit test isolates one piece of logic: arrange inputs, act, assert on the output. Vitest is the Vite-native runner — `describe` groups, `it` defines cases, `expect(result).toBe(expected)` asserts. Fast enough to run on every save.

Good tests assert observable behavior ('given an expired token, isValid returns false'), not implementation details ('it calls parseToken once'). Behavior-based tests survive refactors; implementation-based tests break when the code improves.

Determinism is what keeps a suite trusted: tests touching real time, randomness, or network are flaky by construction. Inject or mock those boundaries (`vi.useFakeTimers()`, `vi.mock(...)`) so the same input always yields the same result.

variants.question: A test for 'trial expires after 14 days' calls the real `Date.now()` and started failing this week — the fixture data aged past the window. What's the durable fix?
options: Control time in the test (fake timers / inject a clock), making the test deterministic regardless of the real date
Widen the assertion to accept both outcomes
Delete the test since expiry logic is simple
Regenerate the fixture data every couple of weeks
variants.rationale: The test depends on wall-clock time — a hidden input that changes daily. Faking time (`vi.useFakeTimers()` + `vi.setSystemTime(...)`) or injecting a clock pins that input, so the test verifies the 14-day rule forever, not just for two weeks after someone refreshes fixtures.
optionExplanations: Correct — remove nondeterminism at the source; time becomes a controlled input.
A test that accepts both outcomes asserts nothing — it's a green light wired to stay green.
Simple logic with real dates is exactly where silent off-by-one expiry bugs live; the test earns its keep.
Scheduled human maintenance to keep a test green is a treadmill — and it *will* be forgotten.
variants.interviewTip: 'How do you deal with flaky tests?' — root-cause categories (time, randomness, network, shared state, order dependence) plus 'make the boundary injectable' is a complete, senior-sounding answer.

variants.question: A test asserts `describe('cart', () => { it('applies a random 5–15% loyalty discount', ...) })` by calling the real `Math.random()` and checking the total is within range. It passes ~99% of runs but fails intermittently in CI with no code change. What's the correct fix?
options: Add a retry so the test re-runs up to three times before it's marked failed
Mock the randomness boundary (e.g. `vi.spyOn(Math, 'random').mockReturnValue(0.5)`) so the discount is a fixed, asserted value
Loosen the range check to 0–100% so the assertion can never fail
Move the test to run only locally, never in CI, since CI machines behave differently
variants.rationale: The flake is nondeterminism from real randomness — a hidden input that varies each run, occasionally landing on a boundary the assertion mishandles. Stubbing `Math.random()` to a fixed value pins the input so the same computation runs every time, turning an intermittent test into a deterministic one that actually verifies the discount formula.
optionExplanations: Retries paper over flakiness — they hide a real nondeterminism bug and let genuinely broken code sneak through on a lucky re-run.
Correct — control the random boundary at the source; the discount becomes a fixed, deterministic input.
A 0–100% range asserts nothing about a 5–15% rule; it's a test wired to always pass.
'Skip it in CI' abandons the coverage exactly where it matters most and doesn't fix the nondeterminism.
variants.interviewTip: Retrying a flaky test is a smell, not a fix. Name the nondeterministic source — here, randomness — and pin it. Interviewers listen for whether you remove the cause or mask the symptom.

sections.heading: End-to-end testing with Playwright
paragraphs: Unit tests check parts; end-to-end tests check the assembled machine: Playwright drives a real browser through real flows — navigate, click, type, assert on what a user would see.

Prefer user-facing selectors — `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })`, `getByLabel('Email')` — over CSS/XPath tied to DOM structure. They survive refactors and double as accessibility checks: if getByRole can't find your button, neither can a screen reader.

Playwright's assertions auto-wait and retry (`await expect(locator).toBeVisible()`), which eliminates the sleep-based flakiness older tools suffered. The testing pyramid still applies: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a thin crust of E2E on the critical paths.

variants.question: Why does Playwright's own documentation push `getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })` over `page.locator('#app > div.form > button:nth-child(3)')`?
options: nth-child is not supported inside locator()
Role selectors execute significantly faster in the browser
Role/name selectors track what users (and assistive tech) perceive, so they survive DOM refactors and implicitly verify accessibility
CSS selectors are deprecated in modern Playwright
variants.rationale: The structural selector encodes today's DOM shape — one wrapper div added and the test lies about the app being broken. The role selector encodes intent ('the button a user knows as Submit'), which changes only when the actual UX changes — and it fails if the button loses its accessible name, catching a11y regressions for free.
optionExplanations: nth-child works fine in locator() — which is part of the problem: it lets you write brittle tests.
Selector speed differences are negligible next to browser and network time.
Correct — resilience to refactors plus built-in accessibility pressure.
CSS selectors remain fully supported; the guidance is preference, not deprecation.
variants.interviewTip: 'How do you keep E2E suites from becoming flaky and hated?' — answer: user-facing selectors, auto-waiting assertions, test isolation, and keeping E2E thin per the pyramid. Four beats, well rehearsed.

variants.question: A test does `await page.waitForTimeout(3000)` then clicks a 'Checkout' button that appears after an async cart load. It passes locally but fails ~10% of the time in CI, where the machine is slower. What's the idiomatic Playwright fix?
options: Wrap the click in a try/catch and retry it in a loop until it succeeds
Disable the test in CI and run it only on the faster local machine
Bump the timeout to `waitForTimeout(8000)` to give the slow CI box more headroom
Replace the fixed sleep with an auto-waiting assertion/locator like `await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click()`, which retries until the element is actionable
variants.rationale: A hardcoded `waitForTimeout` guesses at how long the async load takes — too short and it flakes on slow CI, too long and it wastes time. Playwright's locators and web-first assertions auto-wait and retry until the element is present and actionable, so the test synchronizes on the actual condition instead of a fragile fixed delay. That's the mechanism that kills sleep-based flakiness.
optionExplanations: A manual retry loop reinvents what Playwright's auto-waiting already does, worse and more verbosely.
Skipping in CI abandons coverage on the exact environment where the race actually surfaces.
A bigger fixed sleep just moves the flake threshold and slows every run; it still guesses instead of waiting on the real condition.
Correct — auto-waiting locators retry until the button is actually clickable, eliminating the timing guess entirely.
variants.interviewTip: Any `waitForTimeout` / `sleep` in an E2E test is a red flag. The senior answer: 'wait on a condition, not a duration' — Playwright's auto-waiting assertions do this for you.

sections.heading: CI/CD: the pipeline as gatekeeper
paragraphs: Continuous Integration: every push triggers an automated pipeline — install, lint, type-check, test, build. The point is shrinking the distance between introducing a bug and hearing about it from weeks to minutes.

A typical GitHub Actions flow: on pull request, run the checks; merging is blocked until they're green plus a human review. Continuous Delivery/Deployment extends the green path: merged main auto-deploys to staging, then production — with prod gated manually (Delivery) or fully automatic (Deployment).

Pipelines fail-fast in order of cheapness: lint before tests, unit before E2E. And a red main is a stop-the-line event — the fix or the revert outranks new work, because everyone is building on top of it.

variants.question: A PR's pipeline runs: lint → unit tests → E2E tests → build. E2E is the slowest stage. Why do lint and unit tests run first?
options: Fail fast: cheap checks catch most failures in seconds, so broken pushes don't burn 20 minutes of E2E before reporting the lint error
E2E tests can only run after a deployment to production
Lint must pass before code will compile at all
Alphabetical ordering of pipeline stages
variants.rationale: Pipeline ordering is economics: fastest-and-most-likely-to-fail first. A typo that lint catches in 10 seconds shouldn't cost a full E2E run to discover. Same total coverage, radically better feedback latency for the common failure cases.
optionExplanations: Correct — fail-fast ordering optimizes time-to-feedback, which is the entire point of CI.
E2E runs against a preview or local server in CI — production deployment is not a prerequisite.
Linting is style/correctness analysis, independent of compilation; unlinted code compiles fine.
Stage order is authored deliberately in the workflow file; nothing is alphabetical.
variants.interviewTip: If asked to design a CI pipeline, narrate it in cost order — 'lint, type-check, unit, integration, E2E, build, deploy' — and mention branch protection on green checks. Structure is the signal.

variants.question: Your team's `main` branch pipeline goes red: a merged commit broke the build. A developer opens a fresh PR to add an unrelated new feature and asks to merge it 'since it's green on its own branch'. What does a healthy CI/CD culture do first?
options: Merge the new feature — it's green in isolation, and unrelated to the breakage
Stop the line: fixing or reverting the broken `main` outranks new work, because everyone branches from `main` and builds on the breakage
Disable the failing check on `main` so the pipeline goes green and work can continue
Wait a day to see if the failure resolves itself before taking any action
variants.rationale: A red `main` is a stop-the-line event. Everyone cuts new branches from `main` and merges back into it, so a broken `main` poisons every downstream branch and hides which failures are new. Restoring green — by fixing forward or reverting the offending commit — takes priority over any new feature, however clean that feature looks in isolation.
optionExplanations: Merging onto a broken `main` stacks new work atop the breakage and muddies which failures are the new PR's fault.
Correct — a red shared branch is stop-the-line; fix or revert before new work, because the whole team builds on `main`.
Silencing the check hides the breakage instead of resolving it — the bug ships and trust in the pipeline erodes.
Build failures don't self-heal; waiting just extends the window in which everyone inherits a broken base.
variants.interviewTip: 'Stop the line' is the phrase interviewers want. A red shared branch blocks the whole team, so its fix or revert always outranks new feature work — say that explicitly.
